intro: Today's digest covers critical security patches in OpenSSL, major updates to PostgreSQL and FFmpeg, and the rise of AI-driven hardware design. We also explore new language features in C# and the evolving landscape of privacy and infrastructure.

items.summary: OpenSSL addresses a buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock() via CVE-2026-121481 by returning -1 for invalid inputs, with similar fixes for EVP_DecodeBlock() and base64encode(). Developers should update to prevent potential exploitation via command-line inputs.
items.why: A critical buffer overflow in OpenSSL requires immediate updates to prevent high-severity exploits.

article.title: OpenSSL: Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock() (CVE-2026-121481, CVSS 9.8)

items.summary: PostgreSQL 19 introduces new SQL features like IGNORE NULLS and JSONPath transformations, along with improvements in replication and maintenance. Developers can try these features in a live sandbox environment with real PostgreSQL 19 servers.
items.why: PostgreSQL 19 introduces significant SQL features and JSONPath improvements for backend developers.

article.title: PostgreSQL 19: A hands-on tour with runnable browser examples

items.summary: Frostbite is a new CPU architecture designed and verified by AI, achieving a 4.59x performance-per-watt gain over a modern CPU core. Developers may care as it demonstrates AI's potential to co-design hardware and software, leading to significant performance improvements and new architectural possibilities.
items.why: Frostbite demonstrates how AI can design and verify high-performance CPU architectures.

article.title: Frostbite: A new CPU architecture discovered, designed and verified by AI

items.summary: C# 15 introduces union types, allowing developers to define data structures that can hold one of several possible types. Developers can experiment with these features using a GitHub repository that provides examples and playgrounds for .NET 11 and C# 15.
items.why: C# 15 introduces union types, offering a new way to handle complex data structures.

article.title: C# 15 Unpacked: Unions Have Arrived. Here's Why They Matter
article.summary: All the code in this series is available on GitHub. Clone it, run it, and try breaking it yourself....

items.summary: Signal is blocking AI agents on iOS 27 and Android from accessing its app data to protect user privacy. Developers care because these OS-level AI integrations threaten app-level privacy and limit tools to prevent data exposure.
items.why: Signal is blocking OS-level AI agents to protect app-level user privacy.

article.title: Signal Is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy

items.summary: FFmpeg 9.1 'Gauss' was released on 2026-11-20 as the latest stable version from the 9.1 branch, including updated library versions. Developers should care as it offers new features and security patches, though the development branch is recommended for active contributions and faster bug fixes.
items.why: FFmpeg 9.1 Gauss provides the latest stable updates for multimedia processing and library support.

items.summary: Ankit Gupta used a coding agent to program an FPGA for LLM inference, achieving 213 tokens per second, 33× faster than the baseline. Developers might care as it shows how agents can handle complex hardware programming and optimization, reducing manual effort and cost.
items.why: Shows how coding agents can optimize FPGA hardware for LLM inference at massive speeds.

items.summary: ggml-tpu enables running llama.cpp on Google Cloud TPU by compiling its graph into XLA programs. Developers can leverage TPUs for faster inference with minimal code changes.
items.why: Enables running llama.cpp on Cloud TPUs via XLA for faster model inference.

article.title: llama.cpp on a Cloud TPU: An Unofficial ggml Backend Through XLA
article.summary: ggml-tpu lowers each llama.cpp graph to one StableHLO program, compiles it with XLA and runs it on a TPU through libtpu. Gemma 4 E2B on one TPU v5e chip: build, test every operation, serve, chat, speculative decoding, and a three-cell Colab notebook.

items.summary: A Docker container marked unhealthy continued serving traffic because health checks don't affect traffic routing or restart policies. Developers should understand that health checks only report status, not enforce behavior.
items.why: Clarifies that Docker health checks do not automatically stop containers from serving traffic.

article.title: Marking a container unhealthy didn't stop it from taking traffic
article.summary: I broke a container on purpose and watched Docker mark it unhealthy for 35 seconds while nginx kept sending it a third of all traffic. The actual cause: a missing http_500 in proxy_next_upstream.

items.summary: A language model can rewrite its own weights through self-reasoning without training or gradients, improving accuracy on unseen tasks. Developers may care as this could lead to more efficient, self-improving models that don't require retraining or external prompts.
items.why: New research shows models can rewrite their own weights without traditional training gradients.

article.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
